parties:
Jinnat Ali (Md)  ----- Petitioner 
Vs 
Md Abdu Bakkar Siddique and others  ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Short facts for disposal of this Rule are that the petitioner as pre-emptor sought pre-emption of the impugned Kabala under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as an unnotified co-sharer by inheritance and as a purchaser in the case holding. His further case is, that the opposite party No. 2 sold away the case land by two registered kabalas dated 11-5-1992 in favour of the opposite party No. 1 who is a stranger purchaser in the case holding. 

 3. opposite party No. 1 as pre-emptee contested the case by filing a written objection contending, inter alia that the case is barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties. It has further been alleged that two brothers Abdul Gafur Munshi and Abdul Aziz on purchase of land from the case plot had been in possession and during rent roll operation the names of Abdul Aziz and others were recorded correctly but the name of Abdul Gafur Munshi was recorded wrongly. Abdul Gafur died leaving a widow, a son and 3 daughters and said Abdul Aziz died leaving two sons and a daughter. It is also the case of the opposite) arty No. 1 that his cousin Habibur Rahman transferred some lands in his favour out of the case jote by Heba-bil Ewaz, Exhibit Ka and he also purchased 0.17 acres of land by sale deed No. 8748 dated 20-10-1988 and 0.19 acres by sale deed No. 8466 dated 15-10-88 from the case plot. He has further stated in the written objection that he made improvement of the case land by cutting earth worth Taka 8,000. It is also alleged that although he purchased the case land at a consideration of Taka 25,000 within the knowledge of the petitioner and at his advice he mentioned the purchase value at Taka 6,000 in the kabala and that the present price of the case land is about Taka 35,000. 

 8. The learned Assistant Judge found the case not barred by limitation, nor bad for defect of parties while allowing the pre-emption. He further found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance and also by purchase in the case holding. It is held by him that the petitioner being a co-sharer by inheritance has the highest priority to claim pre-emption in preference to others and in support of his view he relied on the decision reported in 34 DLR 180. The learned Senior Assistant Judge further found that the pre-emptee will not be entitled to get any other price except the kobala price as per section 96(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The learned Assistant Judge, however, assessed the development cost at Taka 5388 which was to be deposited within 30 days by the pre-emptor in favour of the pre-emtee. On the other hand, the learned Subordinate Judge while disposing the appeal concurred with the findings of the learned trial Court on the question of defect of party, limitation and pre-emptees claim of some other price other than the price shown in the Kabala under pre-emption. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, considering the evidence on record reduced the development cost from Taka 5388 to 4000. He further, held that the pre-emptee having acquired his right in the case holding on the basis of a Hiba-Bil-Ewaj, Exhibit Ka, his subsequent purchases of case land by the impugned kabalas under pre-emption are protectable under section 96(10) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and ultimately, he allowed the Appeal reversing the judgment and order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge. 

 9. The moot question that arises now in this Rule is as to whether a transfer by way of simple deed of sale made to a person whose interest accrued in the tenancy prior to such transfer on the basis of a deed of Heba-Bil-Ewaj in lieu of Jainamaj, Tajbih, and the Holy Quran is outside the purview of pre-emption as contemplated under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 11. In the appeal against the aforesaid decision of the lower appellate Court relying on the decision in the case of Munsuruddin Bhuiya vs Md Yakub Ali and others reported in 21 DLR 565 allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge. In this case the pre-emptor having acquired his right in the case holding on the basis of a deed of gift made certain purchases by simple deeds of sales which were ultimately decided as protectable under section 96(10)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, j constituting a Single Bench of this Court. In the case of Golam Mustafa and others vs Kazem Ali Khan @Kazal Khan and others reported in 50 DLR 544 a Single Bench of this Court noticing the decision reported in 11 DLR 353 and discussing the case of Md Azizul Bari vs Md lsmail and another reported in 19 DLR 184 has held the view in the following: 

 13. It is true section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 envisages right of pre-emption to three categories of tenants namely, a co-sharer by inheritance, a purchaser and a contiguous land owner of the land transferred upon deposit of the consideration money of the value of the transferred land as stated in the notice under section 89 or in the deed of transfer together with compensation @ 10% of such amount. But this right has been made excepted in sub-section 10 of section 96 to the five classes of transfers which are not open to pre-emption by anyone claiming under section 96. 

 14. For the reasons as above, it may be held that in the instant case since the pre-emptee's acquisition of interest in the case holding on the basis on non-controversial registered deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj Exhibit Ka, is excepted under section 96(10)( c). So, the subsequent transfers of the case lands to the pre-emptee by the registered sale deeds Exhibit Kha and Gha are outside of the scope of pre-emption. 

 15. It should be mentioned here that a deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj in exchange of jainamaj, Tajbih and the Holy Quran is not a transfer for any pecuniary consideration and, as such, a transfer in a holding by a deed of Heba-Bil-Ewaj within three degrees of relationship by consanguinity between the donee and the donor, is exempted from pre-emption in terms of section 96(10)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. As a sequel to it, any subsequent purchase by the donee, of any land in the said holding is outside the purview of pre-emption as contemplated under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.
